Garuḍa Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda. Its main purpose seems to be to attain freedom from the fear of all poisonous creatures.
There are 25 mantras, mostly in prose.
The science taught here is called ‘gāruḍa-ब्रह्मविद्या’ and is said to have originated from the four-faced ब्रह्मा, the other important teachers being नारद, Bṛhatsena, इन्द्र and भरद्वाज.
Mantras 2 to 4 give the usual prelimi-naries like ṛṣi (sage), छन्दस् (metre), devatā (deity) and viniyoga (usage) as also the nyāsas, purificatory processes of hands and limbs.
Then comes ध्यान or meditation on गरुड or Garutmān (the eagle-mount of Lord विष्णु, known for his stupendous strength and enmity towards the serpents) in a long passage comprising seven verses in the śloka metre. It contains a picturesque description of गरुड who has the famous serpents like अनन्त, वासुकि, तक्षक, Kārkoṭaka and others as his ornaments, all over his body!
This is followed by several mālā-mantras (very long mantras) (mantras 6 to 24) the main purport of them being the destruction (or prayers for destruction) of various kinds of poisons which are described in detail.
The Upaniṣad ends with a phalaśruti, a statement of the favourable results got by the chanting or listening to it.
See also GARUḌA and UPANIṢADS.

Garga
------------------------------------------
There appear to be several sages of this name. The ṛṣi or the sage of the 47th सूक्त of the 6th मण्डल of the Ṛgveda is गर्ग, the son of भरद्वाज.
The woman-sage गार्गी वाचक्नवी mentioned in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.6.1) was a descendant of the sage गर्ग.
The kulapurohita or the family priest of the Yādavas of मथुरा was also a गर्ग. He performed the नामकरण or the naming ceremony of Śrī कृष्ण and बलराम secretly. Again, it was he who advised Vasudeva (their ड़थेर्) to send them to the sage सान्दीपनि for एदुचतिओन्.
The name of गर्ग is mentioned in the list of sages who visited Śrī राम after his return to अयोध्या. It appears in another list too, of sages who visited द्रोणाचार्य in the battlefield of कुरु-क्षेत्र and advised him to retire.
There is also the mention of an astronomer sage गर्ग who performed austerities at Gargasrota on the bank of the river सरस्वती. He discovered the paths of the प्लनेत्स् and the स्तर्स्. Several Gargasaṁhitās are found now. They may all be different versions of an original work.
This गर्ग perhaps lived in 50 B. C. Utpala, the famous commentator of the Bṛhajjātaka of वराहमिहिर (d. A.

) quotes nearly 300 verses from गर्ग’s Saṁhitā. He was the teacher of अत्रि, another well-known sage. The Viṣṇupurāṇa (2.5.26) mentions him as an ancient ṛṣi who had known the consequences of all the nimittas or omens.

Garbhopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda group. It is remarkable for its detailed and accurate description of the development of the garbha or the foetus in the womb. The philosophical part of the work lies in the reflections of the जीव or the individual सोउल् caught in the womb, before birth.
There are 22 mantras, mostly in prose.
First comes an aphoristic description of the human body which is expanded in the next six mantras. The five bhūtas or elements like earth, water and fire, the sense-organs like the eyes and the ears, मिन्द् and intellect, the capacity to know the six kinds of tastes like sweet and sour, voice capable of producing desirable or undesirable sounds—all these are part of the body-system.
The eighth मन्त्र describes how the foetus is formed in the मोथेर्’s womb and how it develops, to become complete by the end of the eighth month. It is interesting to note that according to this Upaniṣad, the जीव (the individual सोउल्) enters the foetus only in the seventh month!
The next मन्त्र dilates upon how a male or a female child—or even a eunuch—as also twins are born.
The verses 10 to 17, give a poignant description of the जीव repenting his miserable state—for being forced to take birth and suffer in numerous lives—due primarily to his own mistake of not seeking God but seeking the transitory pleasures of the world.
However, all this knowledge of his previous lives and the present state is totally forgotten as soon as he is born! (verse 18)
By conceiving of the various parts of the human body as different items in a Vedic sacrifice, the individual can purify his मिन्द् and finally attain लिबेरतिओन्.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Gārgī Vācaknavī
------------------------------------------
Gārgī, daughter of Vacaknu, was the only woman-sage present in the court of the king जनक. She questioned Yājña-valkya, the greatest exponent of the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, of his times, about the warp and woof that links all things. Her learning is representative of the high intellectual standard of the women of the upper classes during the age of the उपनिषद्स्.

Garuḍa
(‘one who flies with the help of wings’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most common and well-known figures that we come across in the Hindu पुराणस् is that of गरुड or Garutmān. He is pictured in a human form, but with two powerful wings and a sharp beak, resembling those of an eagle. He is the वाहन (mount or vehicle) of God विष्णु. He is also shown as the insignia on the banner (dhvaja) of the flagpost of विष्णु temples.
The story of सुपर्ण, the golden winged eagle, bringing the सोम juice from हेअवेन्, as it appears in the Ṛgveda (4.26 and 27) seems to be the basis for the later accounts of गरुड in the epics and the पुराणस्. According to the Ādiparva (chs. 31-34) of the Mahābhārata, गरुड was the son of the sage कश्यप (the progenitor of all living beings) and विनता. Since विनता had become the slave of कद्रू (another wife of कश्यप) due to a curse, गरुड liberated her from it by bringing the अमृत or nectar from हेअवेन्, as per the desire and condition set by कद्रू. (See KUMBHAMELĀ.)
His many heroic exploits so pleased Lord विष्णु that he made गरुड his mount.
In the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, he appears once on the battlefield, when राम, लक्ष्मण and others had become unconscious due to the नागपाश or sarpāstra (snake-missile) discharged by इन्द्रजित्. The serpents immediately fled and they were all back on their feet (vide Yuddhakāṇḍa ch. 50).
In the iconographical works, he is usually depicted as a human figure with powerful and outstretched wings at the back of the two arms, which are in the pose of añjali or obeisance. Sometimes he is shown as flying, carrying विष्णु on his back, his two hands supporting विष्णु’s dangling feet.
The colour of his body may be that of an emerald or pure white. He is also decked with several ornaments.

garbhagṛha
(‘inmost होउसे,’ ‘sanctum sanctorum’)
------------------------------------------
For centuries, हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् have played a very significant part in the spiritual, religious and cultural life of Hindus.
If the temple is the होउसे of God (devālaya = होउसे of God) then, its sanctum sanctorum, technically called ‘garbhagṛha’ or ‘garbhamandira’ is like the drawing room or private living room of God!
The गर्भगृह is generally square in shape with a low roof, with no doors and windows, except for the front opening through which light falls on the image or from which the devotees can have a view of the deity. The roof over the whole shrine is a small tower called ‘vimāna’. This tower is quite high in North Indian temples and of modest height in the South Indian ones.
In some temples a pradakṣiṇapatha—a circumambulatory passage—is provided just round the गर्भगृह, to enable the devotees to go round the deity.

garbhanyāsa
(‘inseminating [the temple site]’)
------------------------------------------
A देवालय or a Hindu temple is not just a place of prayer but a structure where the particular deity ‘lives’ in its subtle body, literally accepting the worship.
An extremely important rite which is performed during the construction of a temple is the गर्भन्यास or inseminating the temple site. A casket or a tray or pot of copper, the dimensions of which are proportional to the dimensions of the temple, is ceremonially lowered into the ground on an auspicious night after filling it with precious stones, several metals, herbs and soils, symbolising च्रेअतिओन् and prosperity. This ceremony is said to help in the smooth consummation of the temple project. A stone called आधारशिला is kept over this spot. This will be the foundation, ultimately, for the installation of the icon.
It is because of this ceremony that the sanctum is called ‘garbhagṛha’.

gārhasthya
(‘the state of being the master of the होउसे’)
------------------------------------------
The वर्ण-आश्रम system was a basic institution that guided the Hindu society during the ancient and medieval days. The वर्ण system, based on the principle of division of labour, helped in the smooth running of the society. The आश्रम system, on the other hand, prepared the individual to become a worthy member of the society first, and later, to transcend it so that the ultimate goal of life—mokṣa or liberation—can be achieved more easily.
Out of the four āśramas—brahmacarya, गार्हस्थ्य, वानप्रस्थ and saṁnyāsa—gārhasthya, the second, has been considered as central, the pivot, of the whole society. This is because the गृहस्थ is the only earning member among all the four groups.
The term ‘gārhasthya’ has been derived from the words ‘gṛha’ (‘house’) and ‘gṛhastha’ (‘one who stays in the होउसे’ or ‘one who is established in the married state’). So, it means the state of the householder.
After finishing his एदुचतिओन् and training in the गुरुकुल, a student (brahmacārin) was expected to return home, marry a suitable girl and raise a family. He thus became a गृहस्थ.
The गृहस्थ was obliged to earn well by dhārmic or right means and live a happy, decent, life which should be socially useful. Among his principal duties were the पञ्चयज्ञस् or the five daily sacrifices. (See PAÑCAYAJÑAS for details.)
Other duties prescribed for him were: eating only twice a day, honouring guests that come to one’s होउसे (especially the holy persons), taking care of the basic needs of all the members of the family and the dependents, treating the elders in the family (like the parents, grand-parents, elder brothers and so on) with due respect and not getting angry with them, and, finally, self-control.

garbharakṣaṇa
(‘protection of the foetus’)
------------------------------------------
Every human being, according to the smṛtis and the धर्मशास्त्रस्, was expected to undergo some सṁस्कारस् or purificatory rites. One of the sixteen such सṁस्कारस् (called ‘ṣoḍaśa-सṁस्कारस्’) is the पुṁसवन rite, of which the rite of गर्भरक्षण is a part.
In this rite, which is meant for protecting the foetus, the husband of the pregnant lady inserts a little dūrvārasa (juice of the grass cynodon dactylon) into her nostril, touches her heart and repeats some mantras such as ‘ā te garbho yonimaitu....’ (Atharvaveda 3.23.2).
This rite is also called ‘anavalobhana’ and is generally done in the fourth month after conception.
See also PUṀSAVANA and ṢOḌAŚA SAṀSKĀRAS.

Gārgya
(‘One who has descended from [the sage] गर्ग’)
------------------------------------------
The धर्मसूत्रस् are early compilations on the various aspects of धर्म. One such ancient work mentioned by famous writers like विश्वरूप (9th century A. D.) is the one by गार्ग्य (a descendant of the sage गर्ग). His original work has not been traced.
The subjects dealt with by this गार्ग्य in his work—as can be gleaned from the questions given by विश्वरूप, अपरार्क (12th century A. D.) and others—are: आह्निक (daily routine), śrāddha (obsequial rites), and प्रायश्चित्त (expiations).
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.1) mentions one ‘Dṛpta-बालाकि गार्ग्य.’ He was a descendant of गर्ग, the son of a lady called Balākā and got the appellation ‘dṛpta’ since he was extremely proud of his learning (dṛpta = proud).
Two more sages known to the Hindu epics and mythological works may also be mentioned here. The first one was the priest of Yudhājit, a prince of the Kekaya kingdom. The second गार्ग्य was the son of the sage Veṇuhotra. He is said to have taught the secrets of धर्म to इन्द्र, the king of the gods in हेअवेन्.

Garuḍapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
For centuries, the purāṇas—stories of the ancient period, mythological lore—have served the purpose of educating the masses, both in the religious and in the secular fields. Recitation and exposition of the पुराणस् in temples and dharmaśālas by a learned ब्राह्मण for the benefit of the masses was a common sight in the towns and villages of India, even a hundred years ago.
Out of the eighteen mahāpurāṇas—all ascribed to the sage Vyāsa—the Garuḍapurāṇa is listed as the seventeenth. It is said to have derived its name from the fact that विष्णु taught it to गरुड (See also GARUḌA.) at his request.
Assigned to the period A.

, the number of ślokas of this purāṇa, as per different compilations and editions, varies from 8000 to 19,000!
Though considered as a spurious Vaiṣṇava work by the scholar-king Ballaḷasena (12th century A. D.) of the Dānasāgara fame, it is a highly revered work even now.
It comprises two parts: the Pūrva-khaṇḍa (with 240 chapters) and the Uttarakhaṇḍa. The latter again, is divided into two sections, called Pretakalpa (42 chapters) and Brahmakhaṇḍa (29 chapters).
The work is encyclopaedic in character. The contents of the two epics, as also of the Harivaṁśa have been retold here.
The topics dealt with in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa can be summarised as follows: च्रेअतिओन् of the world; worship of the deities सूर्य (the Sun-god), शिव, देवी, गणेश, various aspects of विष्णु and also his āyudhas or weapons; योग or meditations based on the Vaiṣṇava view-point; the सन्ध्या ritual; architecture and town-planning; इचोनोग्रफ्य्; दान or gifts; varṇāśramadharmas; sins and their expiations; geographical and cosmological description of the universe; various vratas or religious observances; the solar and the lunar races of kings; incarnations of Lord विष्णु; आयुर्वेद or the science of medicine and surgery; Aśvavidyā or the science of horses; grammar, poetry and rhetoric; aṣṭāṅgayoga (eightfold योग); hymns on various aspects of विष्णु as नरसिṁह or Acyuta; mantras and अस्त्रोलोग्य्.
The subjects discussed in the Pretakalpa are:
exposition of धर्म; causes for various kinds of births; way to the abode of यम, the god of death; description of यम’s world and his affluent palace; rites connected with the death of a person; after-death ceremonies; various types of śrāddhas; सपिण्डीकरण rite (See SAPIṆḌĪ-KARAṆA.); Nārayaṇabali rite; results of good and bad deeds of human beings.
The Brahmakhaṇḍa deals with the following topics: procedure for saluting Śrīhari; the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्; unity of ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव; च्रेअतिओन् of the world; incarnations of विष्णु and लक्ष्मी; the शालग्राम stone; importance of many holy rivers; worship of विष्णु and eulogy of धर्म.
On the whole, this is a very useful work throwing light on several facets of Hindu religion, culture and social conditions.
See also PURĀṆAS.

gārhapatya
(‘belonging to the gṛhapati or the master of the होउसे’)
------------------------------------------
In the Vedic and the epic period, many a द्विज (the ‘twice born’) maintained three sacred fires, ceremonially established. The गार्हपत्य fire was the first, the other two being the आहवनीय and the dakṣināgni.
The गार्हपत्य fire is first established by kindling it with the araṇis (See ARAṆI.) through the process of अग्न्याधान. (See AGNYĀDHĀNA for details.)
The pit for the गार्हपत्य fire is round in shape and one square aratni in area. (An aratni is 1/5 of the height of the sacrificer who establishes the fire.)
The fire itself is used for various purposes such as: daily अग्निहोत्र; warming the हविस् of oblatory material; warming the vessels used for the same; circumambulation; cooking the हविस्; to start the other two fires.
This fire, once kindled, had to be maintained throughout life.
In Somayāgas, another आहवनीय fire is generated from the earlier one, in the उत्तरवेदि (a higher platform to the east). In such a case, the former fire is also called ‘gārhapatya.’
See also PAÑCĀGNI.
